cards.title: Maximum reset threshold of synchronizing automata
cards.formal: For every integer n≥1, determine T(n)=max{rt(A): A is a synchronizing complete deterministic finite automaton with n states and any finite nonempty alphabet}, where rt(A) is its shortest reset-word length.
cards.definitions: An automaton here is a finite transition system A=(Q,Σ,δ), with |Q|=n, a finite nonempty alphabet Σ, and a total function δ:Q×Σ→Q. Extend δ to words by δ(q,ε)=q and δ(q,wa)=δ(δ(q,w),a). A word w is a reset word when |{δ(q,w):q∈Q}|=1. The automaton is synchronizing if at least one such word exists; its reset threshold rt(A) is the minimum number of letters in a reset word. The quantification ranges over every n and every finite alphabet and total transition function satisfying this promise. The common final state need not be specified beforehand. Initial states and accepting states play no role. The empty word handles n=1. No strong-connectivity, binary-alphabet, permutation-letter, or other structural restriction is imposed. Partial automata, nondeterministic transitions, and synchronizing only a prescribed proper subset of Q are different models. The maximum is well-defined: on n labeled states there are only n^n different letter transformations, and duplicate transformations may be removed without changing shortest reset lengths. Thus finitely many transition alphabets suffice. T(1)=0. The target is the integer-valued function of n, not the running time of testing synchronization.
cards.answer_criterion: Specify a real-valued approximation g on the positive integers and prove in Lean that |g(n)−(T(n) : ℝ)|≤1/100 for every integer n≥1, using the model and target defined here. Certified lower and upper functions ℓ(n)≤T(n)≤u(n) with u(n)−ℓ(n)≤1/50 also qualify via their midpoint. The answer may use unambiguous mathematical expressions or certified bounds; g need not be integer-valued, and no simple exact formula for T(n) is required. An exact determination also qualifies. A one-sided bound, agreement at finitely many n, or an asymptotic estimate without the stated pointwise error guarantee does not meet this criterion.
cards.why: A central extremal problem in automata theory, with a simple finite-state formulation and a sharp explicit candidate bound. It tests whether local compression and algebraic structure can force globally short control sequences in every synchronizing system.

importance.reason: The flagship quantitative question about synchronizing automata, connecting finite-state control, extremal combinatorics, and linear-algebraic methods.

progress.text: Černý constructs an n-state family with reset threshold exactly (n−1)², establishing the sharp lower-bound target.
The classical Pin–Frankl compression argument gives a general cubic upper bound; the survey records (n³−n)/6−1 for n≥4.
Szykuła combines compression with avoiding words to improve the long-standing leading cubic constant.
Shitov improves that argument to a leading constant approximately 0.1654; the exponent remains three.
Volkov’s updated list records established special classes and their reset-threshold bounds while keeping the general conjecture open.
Zhu reports a proof for the one-cluster subclass in a preprint. This card does not independently certify that proof or extend it to unrestricted automata.
Szykuła’s AFL 2026 survey explicitly states the general conjecture and identifies the cubic Shitov estimate as the best known unrestricted bound.

context_blocks.text: This card asks for the worst-case reset-length function with absolute approximation error at most 0.01 for every n. The Černý conjecture predicts T(n)=(n−1)². Determining a different function would also answer this card, but merely refuting the conjectured formula would not.

Synchronization asks how to restore a finite system to a known state when its current state is unknown. A fixed input sequence must work simultaneously from every possible starting state; it cannot observe the intermediate state and adapt its next letter. The length bound therefore measures the cost of an open-loop reset, rather than ordinary shortest-path navigation from a known vertex.

The proposed constant is forced by a concrete family. On states 0,…,n−1, let a cyclically increment the state and let b send n−1 to 0 while fixing the other states. For n≥2, the word b(a^{n−1}b)^{n−2} has length (n−1)² and resets this automaton. Černý’s construction also proves that no shorter reset word works. This is the known lower bound for T(n); the Černý conjecture predicts equality for every n.

Knowing that a reset exists is much easier than establishing its sharp maximum length. Pairwise merging gives polynomial criteria for synchronizability, and successive compression of subsets gives general polynomial length bounds. The bottleneck is how much progress one can force as the current set of possible states shrinks. Adding separate worst-case bounds for these stages gives a cubic estimate and can lose information about how the stages interact.

The August 2026 open-problems survey records a general upper bound of approximately 0.1654n³+o(n³), due to Shitov’s refinement of Szykuła’s result. The gap is therefore in the exponent as well as the leading constant: the conjecture asks for the exact quadratic bound (n−1)². Results for restricted transition systems do not establish that bound for all synchronizing automata.

A July 2026 preprint reports the conjectured bound for one-cluster automata: systems having a letter whose functional graph has exactly one directed cycle. Its sharper positive-level estimate uses the cycle length and the distance of off-cycle states from that cycle. This is a claim for a restricted class, and the later general survey still states the unrestricted conjecture as open.

cards.title: Busy Beaver BB(6)
cards.formal: Determine the value of $BB(6)=S(6)$, the maximum number of steps taken before halting by a deterministic Turing machine with six nonhalting states, two tape symbols, and one initially all-zero, bi-infinite tape. The transition into a separate halting state counts as one step. Thus $BB(6)=\max\{T(M):M\in\mathcal{M}_6\text{ halts on the blank tape}\}$, where $T(M)$ counts executed transitions and the machine class is fixed below.
cards.definitions: The states are A, B, C, D, E, F and a separate halting state Z; Z is not one of the six states being counted. Tape cells are indexed by the integers and contain 0 or 1. Initially every cell contains 0, the head is at cell 0, and the state is A. For each nonhalting state and scanned symbol, the transition table specifies a symbol to write, a move by exactly one cell left or right, and a next state. Execution stops on entering Z, including that final write-and-move transition in T(M). Unreachable states are allowed. The finite set of these transition tables is $\mathcal{M}_6$. Here BB is the runtime (maximum-shift) function S, not the function $\Sigma$ that maximizes the number of 1s left on the tape. In the progress note, $2\uparrow\uparrow k$ is a tower of k twos, and $2\uparrow\uparrow\uparrow 1=2$, $2\uparrow\uparrow\uparrow(k+1)=2\uparrow\uparrow(2\uparrow\uparrow\uparrow k)$.
cards.answer_criterion: Specify a real approximation a and prove in Lean that |a−(BB(6) : ℝ)|≤1/100 in the machine model stated here. Equivalently, give certified real bounds ℓ≤BB(6)≤u with u−ℓ≤1/50 and use their midpoint. The approximation or interval may be given by an unambiguous mathematical expression; neither an integer output, a decimal expansion nor a simple exact expression for BB(6) is required. A proof of exact equality also qualifies. An uncertified estimate, a lower bound alone or a bound with a larger error does not meet the criterion.
cards.why: This is a defining concrete problem in computability: identify the longest finite computation possible in a fixed, exceptionally small universal machine formalism. A proof would advance the boundary of complete mathematical understanding of small programs and test methods for nontermination proofs, recurrence analysis, and formal verification. The significance lies in establishing the exact boundary, not merely constructing a machine with an enormous runtime.

importance.reason: A landmark finite problem at the frontier of computability and formal verification, asking for the next binary Busy Beaver runtime value after the resolved five-state case.

progress.text: The project credits mxdys with a six-state halting machine establishing $S(6)>2\uparrow\uparrow\uparrow 5$. This is a lower bound, not an exact determination.

The dated project list records 1,003 BB(6) holdouts after its equivalence reductions. This is a progress report from an informal search, not a certified exact value.

context_blocks.text: Fixing the number of states leaves finitely many machines, so a maximum halting time exists. Nevertheless, enumerating their transition tables does not tell us when to stop waiting for the machines that never halt. The Busy Beaver function packages that obstruction into a sequence of finite integers. Noncomputability of the whole sequence does not prevent individual values from being established.

The five-state case provides a concrete precedent: the bbchallenge collaboration proved S(5)=47,176,870 with the Coq proof assistant. Its proof combines a complete enumeration after symmetry reductions with methods that certify halting or nonhalting. The paper makes precise how a finite search can be accompanied by a universal proof.

Six states introduce obstacles beyond running a larger search. The Antihydra machine has a halting question expressed through an integer recurrence whose parity behavior is still unresolved. A probabilistic heuristic about that behavior is not a proof that the machine runs forever. An exact Busy Beaver bound would also decide its halting behavior in principle, even if the required finite computation were physically infeasible.

The target is the six-state runtime maximum, with benchmark acceptance at absolute error at most 0.01. Runtime and final tape output are different extremal quantities, and machine conventions matter. Existing catalogue questions about Busy Beaver growth, logical thresholds, or population protocols therefore remain separate problems.

cards.definitions: An instance consists of a finite set G of m≥0 indivisible goods and n agents. Each number vᵢg is a nonnegative real, and vᵢ(S)=∑g∈S vᵢg for S⊆G. Let Πd(G) denote all labeled partitions (P₁,…,Pd) of G into d pairwise disjoint bundles, allowing empty bundles. The 1-out-of-d maximin share of agent i is μᵢ(d)=maxP∈Πd(G) min1≤j≤d vᵢ(Pⱼ). The maximum is attained because the set of partitions is finite. A complete allocation A belongs to Πₙ(G): every good goes to exactly one agent, with no copies, payments, disposal or fractional goods. Define Dₙ as the set of positive integers d such that for every m and every valuation table there exists such an A with all n inequalities. Then d*(n)=min Dₙ. Increasing d weakens each benchmark. Known universal upper bounds make Dₙ nonempty, so this minimum is attained. The quantifiers are ∀n, choose d*(n), then ∀instances, ∃allocation; d may not depend on the number or values of the goods. This is an existence extremum, with no computation-time or preference-query restriction.
cards.answer_criterion: Specify a real-valued approximation g on the positive integers and prove in Lean that |g(n)−(d*(n) : ℝ)|≤1/100 for every integer n≥1, using the model and target defined here. Certified lower and upper functions ℓ(n)≤d*(n)≤u(n) with u(n)−ℓ(n)≤1/50 also qualify via their midpoint. The answer may use unambiguous mathematical expressions or certified bounds; g need not be integer-valued, and no simple exact formula for d*(n) is required. An exact determination also qualifies. A one-sided bound, agreement at finitely many n, or an asymptotic estimate without the stated pointwise error guarantee does not meet this criterion.

context_blocks.title: Relax the number of benchmark bundles
context_blocks.text: An agent imagines dividing all goods and then receiving her least valuable bundle. Ordinary MMS uses n bundles, one per real agent. Using a larger imaginary number d lowers the required share, while the actual allocation still has n recipients. The question is how little this benchmark must be weakened to make it universally achievable.

context_blocks.title: A small example
context_blocks.text: If an agent values each of six goods at 1, her 1-out-of-2 share is 3 and her 1-out-of-3 share is 2. Those numbers describe her personal benchmarks, not how many agents must actually receive goods. Different agents can value the same goods differently, so their best benchmark partitions need not coincide.

context_blocks.title: What ordinal means here
context_blocks.text: The fairness comparison is determined by each agent’s ranking of complete bundles. It is preserved if that ranking stays the same. Knowing only an ordering of individual goods does not generally determine the ordering of their sums. Thus this question does not assume an algorithm receives only individual-item rankings.

context_blocks.title: The known denominator bounds
context_blocks.text: For n≥2 the checked results give d*(n)≤min{2n−2, ⌊3n/2⌋, 4⌈n/3⌉}; retaining the minimum handles rounding for small n. The last bound comes from the 2024 result. Trivially d*(1)=1 and d*(n)≥n: with only d<n goods valued at 1 by everyone, a 1-out-of-d guarantee would require a good for every agent. The exact universal denominator remains undetermined.

context_blocks.title: Why the exact threshold matters
context_blocks.text: An exact answer would identify how much competition an indivisible-resource fairness benchmark must tolerate before everyone can be protected. Recent work combines ordinal shares with envy guarantees in restricted preference classes. Those additional guarantees are useful, but they do not settle the unrestricted denominator function asked for here.

cards.title: Minimum cuts for finite envy-free cake-cutting protocols
cards.area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
cards.formal: For each integer n≥1, determine the least integer c*(n) such that some finite deterministic Robertson–Webb protocol always allocates the entire cake envy-freely among n agents using at most c*(n) final cuts, allowing an agent several disconnected intervals.
cards.why: Separates the complexity of an allocation's geometry from the amount of information a protocol obtains.

progress.text: Stromquist rules out finite protocols whose complete envy-free output always uses only n−1 final cuts for n≥3.
Bounded complete-allocation protocols show that a finite uniform cut bound exists for every number of agents.
An exact cut bound is proved for an existential equal-length proportional variant, with different fairness and computational requirements.
A preprint reports single-exponential query complexity for complete envy-free allocation, without optimizing final cuts exactly.

cards.definitions: The cake is [0,1]. Each of n agents has a nonatomic Borel probability measure μᵢ: values are nonnegative and countably additive, μᵢ([0,1])=1, and every point has value zero. A bundle is a finite union of intervals. Its value need not equal its length. The protocol accesses valuations only by exact Robertson–Webb queries: Eval(i,x,y) returns μᵢ([x,y]); Cut(i,x,a), for 0≤a≤μᵢ([x,1]), returns y≥x with μᵢ([x,y])=a. Query endpoints are 0, 1 and earlier cut marks; additivity allows combining known interval values. If a cut has multiple valid answers, correctness must hold for every answer. Finite exact computation on the transcript is allowed without a bit-time bound. The output uses known marks as endpoints. Endpoints themselves may be assigned arbitrarily because they have value zero. Envy-freeness means μᵢ(Aᵢ)≥μᵢ(Aⱼ) for every ordered pair i,j. Proportionality means μᵢ(Aᵢ)≥1/n for every i, measured against the whole original cake. There is no approximation, randomness, density bound or promise that agents agree. The output is a complete partition of the cake into bundles A₁,…,Aₙ. A final cut is an internal endpoint between two positive-length intervals assigned to different agents, after adjacent intervals with the same recipient have been merged. Thus an output with r such successive intervals uses r−1 final cuts; 0 and 1 do not count. Isolated endpoint ownership has no cost or fairness effect. Following the cited Stromquist paper, a point merely queried or marked during the protocol is not a final cut unless it is used as an allocation boundary. A protocol is finite if it terminates after finitely many queries on every profile and every valid sequence of answers. That query count may depend on the valuations and need not be bounded by a function of n; local computation must also terminate. In contrast, the number of final cuts must have the uniform bound c*(n). More formally, c*(n) is the minimum over nonnegative integers c for which such a finite protocol for n agents exists. Bounded complete-allocation protocols show this set is nonempty, so the integer minimum is attained. This question charges output cuts, not evaluation queries, queried marks, or total running time.
cards.answer_criterion: Specify a real-valued approximation g on the positive integers and prove in Lean that |g(n)−(c*(n) : ℝ)|≤1/100 for every integer n≥1, using the model and target defined here. Certified lower and upper functions ℓ(n)≤c*(n)≤u(n) with u(n)−ℓ(n)≤1/50 also qualify via their midpoint. The answer may use unambiguous mathematical expressions or certified bounds; g need not be integer-valued, and no simple exact formula for c*(n) is required. An exact determination also qualifies. A one-sided bound, agreement at finitely many n, or an asymptotic estimate without the stated pointwise error guarantee does not meet this criterion.

context_blocks.title: Questions and physical fragmentation are different costs
context_blocks.text: A protocol can ask an agent to mark many candidate boundaries and then use only a few in the final division. This card follows the source’s explicit convention that cuts are the boundaries actually used. It asks how fragmented a division must become when it also has to be findable through finitely many queries.

context_blocks.title: A simple counting example
context_blocks.text: Suppose four successive intervals go to agents A, B, A and C. There are three final cuts, and A receives a disconnected bundle. If the first two intervals both went to A, their common boundary would disappear when those intervals were merged. Counting marks made during the search would be a different objective.

context_blocks.title: Existence does not imply a finite protocol
context_blocks.text: A complete connected envy-free division exists, using n−1 final cuts. Stromquist shows that no finite protocol can always find one for n≥3. Since every recipient in a complete envy-free division has positive value, an n−1-cut division would give exactly one interval per agent. Thus c*(n)≥n for n≥3, despite the existential n−1 bound.

context_blocks.title: The extremum is finite
context_blocks.text: For n=1 no cut is needed, and for n=2 the standard cut-and-choose protocol uses one final cut. General bounded protocols of Aziz and Mackenzie guarantee a finite number of cuts for every n. The September 2026 single-exponential query claim gives another reported upper bound, but its purpose is query complexity and it does not establish the least final-cut count.

context_blocks.title: A recent exact cut theorem has different requirements
context_blocks.text: The MFCS 2026 equal-length result determines an existential cut bound for proportional division with a prescribed physical length per agent. This question imposes exact envy-freeness and finite oracle computation, with no equal-length requirement. Those distinctions prevent transferring the numerical answer directly.

sentences: The whole cake must be allocated so that every agent prefers her own bundle to anyone else’s.
A finite query protocol may give an agent several intervals and may mark more candidate boundaries than it ultimately uses.
The objective is the smallest worst-case number of final allocation cuts for each n.
Connected envy-free divisions exist, but for n≥3 no finite protocol can always find one.
A real approximation to this cut-count function is accepted with Lean-certified absolute error at most 0.01 for every n; a simple exact expression is not required.

meta.status_scope: No claim of exhaustive open-status verification
methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. We aim for benchmarks of 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. All three use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The possible 1,000-problem expansion has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The targets are 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. Top 100, Top 500 and the possible Top 1000 use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
